stimuli.title: Passage
stimuli.text:
In the eighteenth century, a soloist performing a concerto was expected near the end of a movement to play a cadenza, a passage in which the orchestra fell silent and the soloist elaborated on the movement's themes. Composers usually marked only where the cadenza should begin. What the soloist played was left to the performer, who might improvise on the spot or prepare something in advance. Audiences listened to a cadenza less as a part of the composer's work than as a display of the performer's invention.

Over the following century this arrangement changed. Composers increasingly wrote out their own cadenzas, and performers came to regard the written score as a complete statement of the work. Today most soloists play a cadenza written by the composer or by a famous performer of the past, and a soloist who improvises one is rare enough to be remarked upon. Many music historians describe this shift as a loss: an art of improvisation that once belonged to every trained performer, they argue, was surrendered to the authority of the printed page.

That account is not wrong, but it is incomplete. The written cadenza did not simply replace improvisation; it also changed what audiences could hear. A performer improvising under the pressure of a concert tended to rely on familiar figures, the runs and trills that fit comfortably under the hand. A composer writing a cadenza at a desk could instead build it from the movement's own material, developing a theme in ways that the rest of the movement had only suggested. Some of the most admired cadenzas are admired for precisely this reason: they read less as interruptions than as a culmination of the movement.

None of this means that today's soloists should abandon written cadenzas, nor that they must return to improvising. It means that the history of the cadenza is better told as an exchange than as a loss. Performers gave up one kind of freedom, and listeners gained a kind of coherence that improvisation rarely achieved. A performer who chooses to improvise today is not recovering a lost purity; she is choosing one set of rewards over another.

stimuli.title: Passage
stimuli.text:
Before a jury begins deliberating, the judge reads it a set of instructions that explain the law the jurors must apply. In many courts these instructions are drawn from model texts written decades ago by committees of judges and lawyers. The texts are precise, but their precision is the precision of legal drafting: long sentences, technical terms such as "preponderance of the evidence," and double negatives that a lawyer parses easily and a juror may not parse at all.

Researchers who have tested such instructions on mock jurors have repeatedly found that many jurors misunderstand them. In some studies, a large share of participants could not correctly restate the standard of proof they had just been read. The same studies found that rewritten instructions, using short sentences and everyday words, produced markedly better comprehension without changing the legal rule being explained.

Objections to rewriting have generally taken two forms. The first is that plain language sacrifices accuracy: everyday words, the argument goes, carry connotations that technical terms were chosen to avoid. The second is practical. Model instructions have been tested in appeals for years, and courts know which phrasings survive review. A court that adopts new wording invites appeals arguing that the new text misstates the law.

Neither objection is decisive. The first assumes that technical terms convey their intended meaning to jurors, which is exactly what the research calls into question; a phrase that is accurate on the page but misunderstood in the jury box is not accurate in any sense that matters to a verdict. The second objection has more force, but it describes a cost of transition rather than a permanent defect. Several jurisdictions that adopted plain-language instructions have reported that, after an initial period, appeals based on the new wording became uncommon.

What the objections do show is that rewriting should be done with care. Instructions should be revised by drafting committees that include people trained in testing comprehension, and revised texts should be tried on mock jurors before courts adopt them. Done that way, plain language is not a concession to jurors' limitations. It is the only means of ensuring that the law the jury applies is the law the court intended.

stimuli.title: Passage
stimuli.text:
Beneath many forests, the roots of trees are joined by threads of fungi that wrap around or penetrate the root cells. These mycorrhizal fungi draw sugars from the trees and in return deliver water and mineral nutrients that their threads gather from the soil. Because a single fungus can connect to the roots of several trees, researchers have described forests as linked by underground networks, and some have proposed that trees use these networks to pass resources to one another, with large, established trees supporting seedlings growing in their shade.

The idea has spread well beyond the scientific literature. Popular accounts describe parent trees nursing their offspring and forests behaving like cooperative communities. Several ecologists have recently argued that these accounts have outrun the evidence. They point out that the experiments most often cited were small, that many were carried out in greenhouses or with potted seedlings rather than in mature forests, and that carbon labeled in one tree and later detected in another might have traveled through the soil rather than through fungal threads. In some field studies, moreover, seedlings connected to the network of a large tree grew no better, and sometimes worse, than unconnected seedlings.

These critics do not deny that mycorrhizal networks exist, nor that resources can move through them. Their claim is narrower: that the evidence does not yet show that such transfers are large enough or common enough to shape how forests grow, and that it says nothing about whether trees direct resources toward particular neighbors. A fungus that moves carbon from one root to another may simply be moving it where its own growth requires, with the trees involved playing no active role.

The debate matters beyond botany. Forest managers in some regions have begun to recommend leaving large trees standing during logging partly on the ground that they nourish the surrounding seedlings. There may be good reasons for that practice, since large trees provide shade, seed and habitat. But if the practice is to be justified by the network hypothesis in particular, the hypothesis will need to be tested where it would be applied: in mature forests, over years, with measurements designed to tell transfer through fungi from movement through soil.

stimuli.title: Passage A and Passage B
stimuli.text:
**Passage A**

Most scientific research is paid for by taxpayers, yet much of it is published in journals that charge readers for access. A nurse who wants to read a study of the treatment she gives every day, or a teacher who wants to check a claim about how children learn to read, may face a fee for each article. This arrangement makes the public pay twice: once to fund the research and again to read its results. Research funded by public money should be free to read as soon as it is published. Funding agencies can make this happen simply by requiring it as a condition of their grants.

**Passage B**

Few people dispute that publicly funded research ought to be freely available. The difficulty lies in how the costs of publishing are paid once readers no longer pay them. Editing, peer review and hosting are not free, and many journals that have dropped reader fees now charge authors a fee for each article they publish. For a well-funded laboratory such fees are a small line in a grant. For a researcher at a poorly funded university, or in a country where the fee equals months of salary, they can decide whether a study is published at all. A rule that makes articles free to read without asking who pays to publish them may simply move the barrier from the reader to the author. Funders that require open access should also pay, or arrange waivers for, the fees their requirement creates.

stimuli.title: Passage
stimuli.text:
For decades, employers that offered retirement savings plans asked workers to sign up if they wished to take part. Many did not, even when the employer matched part of each contribution, which amounted to turning down free money. Economists working in the field now known as behavioral economics proposed a simple change: enroll workers automatically and let anyone who prefers not to save opt out. Studies of employers that made this switch found that participation rose sharply, especially among younger and lower-paid workers, who had been least likely to sign up on their own.

The result was widely celebrated as proof that small changes in how choices are presented can do what years of education campaigns had not. It also seemed to settle an old argument. If people were the careful planners that standard economic theory assumed, the form on which a choice appeared should not have mattered. That it mattered so much suggested that inertia, not considered preference, had been keeping many workers out of their plans.

Later research complicated the celebration. Automatic enrollment requires the employer to choose a default contribution rate, and most chose a low one. Workers who were enrolled automatically tended to stay at that rate for years, whereas many who had enrolled on their own had chosen higher rates. In some firms, the switch raised the number of savers while lowering the amount the typical saver put aside. The same inertia that brought people into the plan, in other words, kept them at whatever level the plan set for them.

None of this shows that automatic enrollment was a mistake. It shows instead that a default is never neutral. Whoever sets it is making a decision on behalf of the many people who will never change it, and that decision deserves the same scrutiny as any other policy choice. Some employers have responded by raising the default rate gradually each year unless a worker objects, an approach that keeps the advantages of inertia while pointing it toward a more adequate level of saving.

stimuli.title: Passage
stimuli.text:
Eyewitness identifications have long been among the most persuasive evidence a jury can hear. When a witness points to a defendant in court and declares that she is certain, jurors tend to believe her. Yet studies of convictions later overturned by DNA evidence have found that mistaken identifications played a part in a large share of them, and in many of those cases the witness had been confident at trial.

Such findings led many researchers to conclude that a witness's confidence tells us little about whether she is right. That conclusion has since been revised. The problem, more recent work suggests, lies less in confidence itself than in when it is measured. A witness's confidence at trial, often months after the crime, can be inflated by many things that have nothing to do with memory: repeated questioning, learning that the person she chose has been charged, or simply seeing the defendant again and again in the courtroom. Confidence recorded at the first identification, before any of these influences, appears to be a far better guide. In laboratory studies and in some field data, witnesses who expressed high confidence at an initial, fairly conducted lineup were usually correct, while those who hesitated were often wrong.

The word "fairly" carries much of the weight. A lineup is fair when the officer running it does not know which person is the suspect, when the other people in it match the witness's description, and when the witness is told that the culprit may not be present. Departures from these practices can push a witness toward a choice and can raise her confidence in it, which is why researchers urge that her words be recorded at once and in her own terms.

The revised view does not make eyewitness evidence safe. It does give courts a way to tell stronger identifications from weaker ones. Rather than asking how certain a witness is on the stand, a court can ask how certain she was the first time, and under what conditions she was asked.

stimuli.title: Passage
stimuli.text:
Many small songbirds that migrate long distances do most of their traveling at night, even though they are active by day for the rest of the year. Ornithologists have offered several explanations for this habit, and they are not mutually exclusive.

One explanation concerns the birds' bodies. Flight is strenuous and produces heat, and a small bird flying in the warmth of the day loses water quickly as it works to stay cool. The cooler, calmer air of night lets it fly with less water loss and often with less turbulence. A second explanation concerns time. A bird that flies by night can spend the following day feeding, rebuilding the fat that fuels its next flight; a bird that flew by day would have to feed in the dark, which most songbirds cannot do well. A third concerns predators. Hawks and falcons hunt by day, so a songbird crossing open country at night is less exposed to them.

Navigation adds a further consideration. Experiments with caged birds have shown that some species can orient themselves by the pattern of stars around the celestial pole, and many also sense the earth's magnetic field. Night flight would let a bird use the stars directly, though birds kept under overcast skies often orient correctly as well, which suggests that the stars are one cue among several rather than a requirement.

What the explanations share is that each identifies a benefit of flying at night without showing that the benefit is large enough, on its own, to account for the behavior. Testing them against one another is difficult, because the conditions that make night flight cooler also tend to make it safer and to free the day for feeding. Some researchers have turned to the exceptions for help. Species that migrate by day, such as many hawks and swallows, either soar on rising warm air or feed while they fly. Their behavior suggests that the decisive question for a migrant may be whether it can refuel in the air: a bird that cannot must save its days for eating.

stimuli.title: Passage A and Passage B
stimuli.text:
**Passage A**

A translator's first duty is to the words of the original. Readers who pick up a translation are entitled to assume that what they read is what the author wrote, as nearly as another language allows. When translators smooth an awkward sentence, replace a puzzling image with a familiar one or quietly drop a joke that does not carry over, they substitute their own judgment for the author's. A faithful translation may sometimes read stiffly, but its stiffness is honest: it shows readers where the original is strange instead of hiding the strangeness from them.

**Passage B**

Every translator must decide what to be faithful to. A poem that rhymes, a novel narrated in rapid slang or a play whose humor depends on puns cannot keep both its literal sense and its effect in another language. A translator who keeps every word of a joke but loses the laugh has preserved the joke's parts while losing the joke. Readers of the original did not experience the work as strange; they found it funny, or moving, or fast. A translation that leaves its readers puzzled where the original's readers laughed has misrepresented the work, however closely it follows the words. The translator's task is to give new readers an experience as close as possible to the one the author gave the first readers.

stimuli.title: Passage
stimuli.text:
Varnish was applied to old paintings to protect them and to deepen their colors, but most traditional varnishes yellow and darken as they age. A landscape that left the painter's studio with a pale blue sky may now show a sky the color of weak tea. For this reason, conservators have long removed old varnish and applied fresh varnish that stays clear. How far that removal should go, however, has been argued over for generations.

One school of conservators holds that cleaning should be complete. On this view, every layer added after the painter finished, including all old varnish, obscures the work, and a conservator who leaves some in place is substituting a guess about the painter's taste for the evidence of the paint itself. Advocates of complete cleaning point out that partly cleaned pictures often end up with a uniform golden tone that has more to do with later collectors' preferences than with anything the painter intended.

A second school favors leaving a thin layer of old varnish. Its members argue that some painters finished their work with thin, tinted glazes that soften transitions between colors, and that these glazes can be difficult to tell apart from varnish laid on top of them. A conservator who removes everything, they warn, may remove part of the painting along with the varnish, leaving colors that are harsher and more abrupt than the painter ever saw. Cleaning by stages, with pauses to judge the effect, is in their view the only safe course.

The dispute is sometimes presented as one between science and taste, with complete cleaning on the side of science. That description is misleading. Both schools appeal to evidence about how paintings were made, and both must make judgments the evidence does not settle. Advances in analysis have narrowed the disagreement: conservators can now often detect, under magnification and with chemical testing, whether a given layer contains the materials of a glaze or of a varnish. Where such tests are clear, the choice largely makes itself. Where they are not, the conservator still has to decide which risk is worse, leaving too much or taking away too much.

stimuli.title: Passage A and Passage B
stimuli.text:
**Passage A**

Most cities price curb parking far below what drivers are willing to pay, and the result is not cheap parking but scarce parking. When every space on a busy block is full, drivers circle in search of one, adding traffic, burning fuel and delaying buses. A city can do better by setting each block's price according to demand, raising it where spaces are always full and lowering it where they sit empty, with the aim of keeping one or two spaces open on every block. Drivers who most need to park nearby can then find a space, and those who do not can park a few blocks away or travel another way.

**Passage B**

Three years ago the city of Delford began adjusting parking prices block by block every two months, aiming to leave about one space in eight open. On the busiest blocks downtown, prices rose sharply in the first year, while prices on many outlying blocks fell. City surveys found that the time drivers spent searching for parking downtown fell by about a third, and bus delays on the main shopping street became less frequent. The program also drew complaints. Workers at downtown shops, many of them paid hourly, said the new prices took a large share of their wages, and some business owners worried that higher prices would drive customers away, though downtown sales did not fall. In its third year the city began offering discounted monthly permits to low-wage downtown workers, paid for with part of the new parking revenue.

questions.passage: Many residents complain that the city's new bus lanes slow car traffic. Yet since the lanes opened, the average commute for bus riders has become eleven minutes shorter, and bus ridership has risen by a fifth. Car commutes, meanwhile, have grown by only two minutes on average. The bus lanes, therefore, have made commuting in the city better on the whole.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?
options: The bus lanes have drawn more people to ride the bus.
The bus lanes have improved commuting in the city overall.
Complaints that the bus lanes slow car traffic are unfounded.
Car commutes have grown only slightly since the lanes opened.
Bus riders now have shorter commutes than they did before.
questions.explanation: The other claims are offered as support, and "therefore" introduces the claim that commuting is better on the whole. The argument does not call the complaints unfounded: it grants that car commutes grew a little.

questions.passage: Every tenor in the Larkin Choir plays an instrument, and everyone in the choir who plays an instrument rehearses on Tuesday evenings. No one who rehearses on Tuesday evenings serves on the choir's planning committee. Sofia serves on the planning committee.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
options: No one on the planning committee plays any instrument.
Sofia sings a part other than tenor in the choir.
Everyone who rehearses on Tuesdays is a tenor.
Some committee members play an instrument in the choir.
Sofia is not a tenor in the Larkin Choir.
questions.explanation: A tenor in the choir would play an instrument, so would rehearse on Tuesdays, so could not serve on the committee; Sofia serves, so she is not a tenor there. Nothing says she belongs to the choir at all, so the claim that she sings another part need not be true.

questions.passage: The Hartwell Library, now open only Monday through Friday, will begin opening on Sundays next spring. Its director predicts that the number of books borrowed each year will rise as a result, since many residents work during the week and cannot reach the library while it is open.
questions.stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?
options: Opening on Sundays will cost the library less than it expects to gain.
No other library in the area is open to the public on Sundays.
Some residents who cannot visit on weekdays would borrow books on Sundays.
Residents who work during the week read more than other residents do.
Most of the library's current borrowers would prefer to come in on Sundays.
questions.explanation: The prediction rests on residents who cannot come on weekdays. If none of them would come and borrow on Sundays, the stated reason gives no support for a rise. Current borrowers' preferences and other libraries' hours are not needed.

questions.passage: A survey found that employees at firms with free on-site gyms take fewer sick days than employees at firms without them. A consultant concludes that a firm can reduce its employees' sick days by installing an on-site gym.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
options: Firms with gyms tend to hire younger staff, who take fewer sick days anywhere.
Employees who use on-site gyms most often take the fewest sick days of anyone.
Firms without gyms often give employees discounts at nearby gyms.
Installing a gym costs most firms less than the wages lost to sick days.
Employees at firms with gyms report higher job satisfaction than others.
questions.explanation: If gym firms simply employ younger people, the difference in sick days may come from age, not the gym, so installing one need not help. Heavy gym users taking the fewest sick days would point the other way.

questions.passage: Every successful restaurant in Millbrook advertises on local radio. Tanya's new cafe in Millbrook advertises on local radio, so it is sure to succeed.
questions.stem: The argument's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument:
options: takes for granted that the cafe's prices match its competitors'
ignores that some radio stations reach larger audiences than others
assumes that what holds true in Millbrook holds in every other town
treats a feature successful places share as enough to ensure success
relies on restaurant owners who profit from radio advertising
questions.explanation: That all successful restaurants advertise on radio makes radio advertising at most a common feature of success, not a guarantee of it; many restaurants that advertise could still fail. The argument never reasons about other towns or prices.

questions.passage: Principle: A person who borrows an item should return it in the condition in which it was lent, unless the lender agreed in advance to accept it in some other condition.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
options: Lena returned a borrowed coat with a torn lining but offered to pay for the repair, so she acted properly.
Ines repainted a borrowed ladder after its owner agreed beforehand that she could, so she acted properly.
Sam's brother accepted a dented pot after Sam returned it that way, so Sam acted properly.
Rosa returned a borrowed car with less fuel than it had, so the lender acted improperly.
Marco returned a borrowed bicycle with a tire that went flat on its own, so he acted properly.
questions.explanation: The owner agreed in advance to the new condition, which is the principle's exception, so returning the ladder repainted was proper. The bicycle and coat came back changed without prior agreement, and the brother's agreement came only after the fact.

questions.passage: Some critics argue that the town should not restore the old mill because restoration would be costly. But the cost argument ignores the visitors the mill would draw. A restored mill in a similar town nearby attracts thousands of tourists each year, and their spending more than covers the mill's upkeep. So the town should restore its mill.
questions.stem: The claim that a restored mill in a nearby town attracts thousands of tourists each year plays which one of the following roles in the argument?
options: It is the main conclusion that the argument is intended to support.
It is an objection to the conclusion that the argument then answers.
It is a claim that the argument attributes to the critics it opposes.
It is evidence that restoration would cost less than critics claim.
It is offered as evidence that a restored mill could pay its own way.
questions.explanation: The nearby mill's visitors and their spending support the point that a restored mill can cover its costs, which answers the critics. The argument never says restoration itself would be cheaper than claimed.

questions.passage: Any plant that tolerates both shade and dry soil will thrive in the north garden. Every shade-tolerant plant in the Wexley nursery's catalog also tolerates dry soil. Therefore, the bleeding heart listed in the catalog will thrive in the north garden.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
options: The bleeding heart blooms in early spring.
Some plants in the catalog tolerate shade.
The bleeding heart tolerates shade.
Every plant thriving there tolerates shade.
The bleeding heart tolerates dry soil.
questions.explanation: If the bleeding heart tolerates shade, the catalog premise gives it dry-soil tolerance too, and the first premise then guarantees it thrives. Tolerating dry soil alone leaves shade open.

questions.passage: Researchers gave one group of commuters noise-canceling headphones to wear on the train and gave another group nothing. After a month, the headphone group reported less fatigue at work than the other group. The researchers concluded that reducing noise during the commute lowers fatigue during the workday.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
options: At the outset, the groups had similar commutes, jobs and sleep habits.
Noise-canceling headphones are too expensive for many commuters.
Most people in the headphone group listened to music through them.
People in the headphone group knew the study was about fatigue.
Some commuters without headphones also reported less fatigue.
questions.explanation: If the groups were alike at the start, the difference in fatigue is more likely due to the headphones' noise reduction. Music listening or knowing the study's aim would suggest other explanations and so weaken it.

questions.passage: In a regional study, apple orchards bordered by hedgerows received more visits from wild bees than orchards without hedgerows. Among orchards that did not rent honeybee hives, those bordered by hedgerows also produced larger apple harvests.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
options: Orchards bordered by hedgerows rent fewer honeybee hives.
Renting honeybee hives lowers the number of wild bee visits.
Wild bees pollinate apple blossoms better than honeybees do.
Wild bees may add to yields in orchards that rent no honeybees.
Planting hedgerows would raise the harvest of any apple orchard at all.
questions.explanation: Where no honeybees were rented, hedgerow orchards had both more wild bee visits and bigger harvests, which supports a role for wild bees there. The study says nothing about orchards that rent hives, so claims about every orchard or about honeybees go too far.

questions.passage: An online poll on a cycling club's website asked whether the city should build more bike lanes, and 92 percent of those who responded said yes. Clearly, the great majority of the city's residents want more bike lanes.
questions.stem: The argument's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument:
options: ignores the cost to the city of building more bike lanes
relies on a sample unlikely to represent the city's residents
treats a widely held opinion as though it were a proven fact itself
fails to say how many bike lanes the city already has built
assumes that residents who want bike lanes will use them
questions.explanation: People who answer a poll on a cycling club's site are likely to be cyclists, so their views say little about residents as a whole. The conclusion is about what residents want, so it does not treat an opinion as a fact.

questions.passage: After the town of Elmford lowered the speed limit on its main road from 40 to 30 miles per hour, the number of crashes on that road rose, even though average driving speeds on the road fell.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
options: Drivers in Elmford had complained about the lower limit in advance.
Crashes at lower speeds tend to cause fewer serious injuries than others.
Nearby towns that kept their speed limits saw no change in crashes.
Most drivers on the main road obeyed the new lower limit once it took effect.
At the same time, a large school reopened on the road, adding heavy traffic.
questions.explanation: Much heavier traffic at drop-off times could raise the number of crashes even as speeds fell, so both facts can be true. Less serious crashes would not explain more of them.

questions.passage: Columnist: The city's plan to plant 10,000 street trees will not cool the city's hottest neighborhoods. The planting sites were chosen mainly in neighborhoods that already have the most trees.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the columnist's argument?
options: Street trees are the most effective means of cooling a hot city neighborhood.
The planting sites were chosen to please residents of wealthy neighborhoods.
The hottest neighborhoods are not mainly those that already have the most trees.
Neighborhoods with many trees are cooler than any others in the city.
Some of the new trees will die before they are large enough to give shade.
questions.explanation: If the hottest neighborhoods were the ones already full of trees, planting there would reach them and the argument would fail. The claim that treed areas are the coolest of all is stronger than the argument needs.

questions.passage: Legislator: My opponent says the proposed tax credit will mostly benefit wealthy households, because wealthy households pay more tax. But last year she voted for a mortgage deduction that, by the same reasoning, mostly benefits wealthy households, and she described that deduction as a measure for the middle class.
questions.stem: The legislator responds to the opponent by:
options: arguing that the opponent applies her reasoning inconsistently
showing that the opponent's conclusion rests on a false premise
questioning the accuracy of the opponent's figures on tax paid
suggesting that the opponent has a personal stake in the vote
offering evidence that the tax credit will help the middle class
questions.explanation: The legislator says the opponent's reasoning would condemn a measure she praised, which charges her with inconsistency. No evidence about who the credit helps is offered, and the premise about tax paid is not disputed.

questions.passage: Every exhibit in the west wing of the Halden Museum was donated to the museum. Some of the donated exhibits are on loan to other museums. None of the exhibits on loan is insured by the Halden Museum.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
options: None of the donated exhibits is insured by the museum.
Some exhibits in the west wing are on loan to other museums.
Every exhibit in the west wing is insured by the museum.
Some donated exhibits are not insured by the Halden Museum.
Every exhibit the museum does not insure is on loan.
questions.explanation: Some donated exhibits are on loan, and nothing on loan is insured by Halden, so those donated exhibits are uninsured. The loaned exhibits need not come from the west wing, so nothing follows about that wing.

questions.passage: Whenever the river floods, the ferry stops running. The ferry ran this morning, so the river did not flood this morning.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
options: Usually when the gallery holds an opening, the cafe stays open late. It closed early tonight, so there was probably no opening.
Whenever the gallery holds an opening, the cafe stays open late. The cafe closed early tonight, so there was no opening tonight.
Whenever the gallery holds an opening, the cafe stays open late. There was no opening tonight, so the cafe closed early tonight.
Whenever the gallery holds an opening, the cafe stays open late. There was an opening tonight, so the cafe is open late every night.
Whenever the gallery holds an opening, the cafe stays open late. The cafe stayed open late tonight, so there was an opening tonight.
questions.explanation: The ferry argument reasons from the absence of the result to the absence of its condition, and so does the cafe that closed early. The no-opening version reasons from the absent condition, and the late-night version from the present result, both invalid.

questions.passage: Each ingredient in Chef Ola's new dish is one that food critics have praised. So the critics are sure to praise the new dish.
questions.stem: The argument's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument:
options: relies on the opinions of critics instead of those of diners
confuses a dish's popularity with the quality of its cooking
assumes that the chef's past success guarantees future praise
fails to say which critics praised which of the ingredients
presumes a whole has a quality that each of its parts has
questions.explanation: Praised ingredients can still be combined into a dish that critics dislike, so a quality of each part does not pass to the whole. The argument makes no claim about the chef's earlier dishes.

questions.passage: City planners propose cutting downtown parking fees in half in order to bring more shoppers downtown. They argue that many shoppers now avoid downtown because parking there is expensive.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would it be most useful to determine in order to evaluate the planners' proposal?
options: Whether city officials themselves usually shop downtown
Whether downtown stores charge more than suburban stores do
Whether downtown parking is already full at peak shopping times
How much revenue the city now earns from parking tickets
How long downtown parking fees have stayed at the current level
questions.explanation: If the spaces are already full when people shop, cheaper parking cannot let more shoppers park, and the plan fails; if there are empty spaces, it may work. The age of the current fees bears on neither outcome.

questions.passage: Any law that both major parties have publicly supported will survive the coming change of government. The new water-safety law was drafted by a committee whose members came from both major parties. Therefore, the water-safety law will survive the coming change of government.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
options: Every law drafted by a committee from both parties has been publicly backed by both.
Both major parties have publicly supported at least some laws on water safety.
Only laws publicly supported by both major parties survive a change of government.
The members of the drafting committee were respected within their own parties.
Laws that one of the major parties openly opposes rarely survive a change of government.
questions.explanation: With that assumption the law counts as one both parties have supported, and the first premise then guarantees it survives. The claim that only such laws survive states a requirement, not a guarantee.

questions.passage:
Ana: Public libraries should stop buying printed reference books. Nearly all of the information in them is available free online.

Bo: Not everyone has reliable internet access, and for many such people printed reference books in a library are the only free source of that information.
questions.stem: The dialogue most strongly supports the claim that Ana and Bo disagree over whether:
options: nearly all reference information is available free online
everyone in the community has reliable internet access
the reference information found online is usually accurate
public libraries should stop buying printed reference books
public libraries ought to provide information free of charge
questions.explanation: Ana says libraries should stop buying such books, and Bo gives a reason they should keep doing so. Bo never disputes that the information is online, and Ana says nothing about who has internet access.

questions.passage: Every member of the Pike Hiking Club who has climbed Mount Ardel has also climbed Mount Brisk. Some members who have climbed Mount Brisk have not climbed Mount Corin. No member who has climbed Mount Corin has climbed Mount Ardel.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true of the club's members?
options: One member has climbed only Mount Brisk of the three.
One member has climbed all three of the mountains.
Some Ardel climbers have never climbed Mount Corin.
Every Corin climber has also climbed Mount Brisk.
No member has climbed Mount Ardel at any time.
questions.explanation: Climbing all three would mean climbing both Corin and Ardel, which the third statement rules out. Each other option is consistent with every statement; for instance, Corin climbers may well have climbed Brisk too.

questions.passage: Last year, 30 percent of the bicycles stolen in Carville were stolen from the train station, up from 20 percent the year before. So more bicycles were stolen from the train station last year than the year before.
questions.stem: The argument's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument:
options: takes for granted that stolen bicycles were not found
ignores that some thefts are never reported at all
assumes the station is less secure than other places
relies on figures from a period of only two years in one town
overlooks that the total number of thefts may have fallen
questions.explanation: A larger share of a smaller total can be a smaller number: 30 percent of 100 thefts is fewer than 20 percent of 200. Unreported thefts would affect both years and do not touch the step from shares to numbers.

questions.passage: Ecologist: The Cray River's salmon have declined sharply since the river's dam was built, because the dam keeps salmon from reaching their upstream spawning grounds. So once the planned fish ladder lets salmon pass the dam, the decline will reverse.
questions.stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?
options: The dam was built chiefly to generate electricity for the region.
No other river in the region has lost as many salmon in that time.
The upstream spawning grounds are still fit for salmon to spawn in.
The fish ladder will be built before the salmon decline any further.
Salmon that pass the dam will return to the same grounds every year.
questions.explanation: If the upstream grounds can no longer support spawning, letting salmon reach them would not reverse the decline. Returning to the same grounds every year is more than the argument needs, and the timing of construction is not required.

questions.passage: Studies show that people who drink green tea every day have lower rates of heart disease than people who do not. A supplement company concludes that its green tea extract pills will lower the risk of heart disease for people who take them.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
options: The compounds in tea linked to heart health are lost in making the extract.
Rates of heart disease have fallen in the general population lately.
The extract pills cost more each month than a daily cup of green tea.
Many people who dislike the taste of green tea would rather take a daily pill.
The tea drinkers in the studies came from a wide range of countries.
questions.explanation: If the protective compounds do not survive into the extract, the pills lack what tea drinkers get, so the studies give no reason to expect a benefit. Price and taste do not affect whether the pills work.

questions.passage: Most members of the town council are lawyers, and most lawyers in town support the new zoning plan. So most members of the town council support the new zoning plan.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in the argument above is most similar to that in which one of the following?
options: Most teachers in the city are vegetarians, and most guests were vegetarians. So most guests at the party were teachers.
Most guests at the party were teachers, and no teachers in the city eat meat. So most guests did not eat meat.
All guests at the party were teachers, and all teachers in the city are vegetarians. So all guests were vegetarians.
Most guests at the party were teachers, and most teachers in the city are vegetarians. So most guests were vegetarians.
Most guests at the party were teachers, and some teachers in the city are vegetarians. So some guests were vegetarians.
questions.explanation: Both arguments move from most of a group being X and most X being Y to most of the group being Y, which fails because the councillors or guests could be among the minority. The all-guests and no-meat versions are valid.

questions.passage: Sea otters returned to Morrow Bay several years after a ban on trapping them. Over the same period, the bay's kelp forests, which had nearly vanished, grew back. Marine biologists conclude that the otters helped the kelp recover by eating sea urchins, which graze on kelp.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
options: Kelp forests give shelter to many kinds of fish that live in the coastal waters.
In nearby bays where otters did not return, urchins stayed plentiful and kelp sparse.
Water temperatures in the bay rose slightly over the same period of years.
Sea otters eat many kinds of shellfish besides sea urchins whenever urchins are scarce.
Before the ban, trappers had taken most of the otters that lived in Morrow Bay.
questions.explanation: Bays without returning otters act as a comparison: if their urchins stayed and kelp did not recover, the otters' return is the likely difference. Warmer water would suggest another cause.

questions.passage: Many people assume that a novel translated into dozens of languages must be well written. Yet whether a novel is translated depends largely on whether publishers expect it to sell, and publishers often bet on books that resemble earlier hits. The number of translations, then, tells us more about a book's expected market than about the quality of its writing.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?
options: Whether a novel is translated depends largely on sales forecasts.
Novels translated into many languages are usually poorly written.
Readers should not trust publishers' choices about what to translate.
Publishers prefer to translate novels that resemble earlier hits.
Translations reflect a novel's expected sales more than its quality.
questions.explanation: "Then" marks the final sentence as the conclusion, supported by the claims about publishers. The argument never says widely translated novels are badly written, only that translations do not show quality.

questions.passage: Dana Reyes, one of the most respected chefs in the country, says that the new cholesterol drug is unsafe. Given her reputation, the drug must be unsafe.
questions.stem: The argument's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument:
options: assumes that all respected chefs hold the same opinion as hers
confuses how respected a person is with how popular she is
treats someone as an authority on a subject beyond her expertise
fails to say which side effects the drug is supposed to cause in patients
draws a general conclusion about drugs from a single drug alone
questions.explanation: A chef's reputation rests on cooking, which gives no special standing on drug safety. The argument concludes only about this one drug, so it makes no general claim about drugs.

questions.passage: To reduce litter on its trails, the park district will place more trash cans along them. This will work, because most of the litter on the trails is dropped by hikers who cannot find a trash can nearby.
questions.stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?
options: Some hikers who now drop litter would use a nearby trash can.
The park district has tried other ways to cut litter without success.
Trash cans reduce litter more than signs asking hikers not to litter.
Litter on the trails harms wildlife more than litter found elsewhere.
Most of the park's visitors use the trails rather than other areas.
questions.explanation: If hikers who now drop litter would not use nearby cans either, adding cans would change nothing. Whether cans beat signs is beside the point: the argument claims only that cans will work.

questions.passage: Editor: Our newspaper should not publish the leaked memo. Although it is newsworthy, publishing it would reveal the name of a junior employee who did nothing wrong and who could lose her job as a result.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the editor's reasoning?
options: A paper should publish any newsworthy material once it has confirmed that the material is genuine.
A paper should weigh a story's public interest against the harm it might do to the paper itself.
Newsworthiness should be the most important factor in a paper's decisions about what to print.
A paper should not publish what would seriously harm a blameless person, even if newsworthy.
A paper should protect the identity of anyone who gives it a leaked document to publish.
questions.explanation: The editor grants the memo is newsworthy but declines because a blameless employee could be harmed, which is exactly the principle. The employee named is not described as the leaker, so protecting sources does not fit.

questions.passage: Since the city replaced its streetlights with brighter LED lamps two years ago, reported burglaries in residential areas have fallen by a quarter. The mayor credits the brighter lights for the decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
options: The new LED lamps use much less electricity than the lamps they replaced did.
In those two years, the city doubled its nightly police patrols in residential areas.
Some burglaries in the city are never reported to the police at all.
Most burglaries in the city's residential areas take place after dark.
Residents of several neighborhoods complained that the new lamps were far too bright to sleep.
questions.explanation: Doubled patrols at night offer another explanation for the drop, so the lights may not deserve the credit. That most burglaries happen after dark makes lighting more relevant, which supports the mayor.

questions.passage: Each of the five finalists in the Brook County essay contest is a high school senior. Every high school senior in the contest wrote about local history. Two of the finalists also entered the county's poetry contest.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
options: Every essay about local history was written by a finalist.
Everyone who entered the poetry contest is a high school senior.
No one who wrote about local history entered the poetry contest.
Three of the five finalists did not write about local history.
At least two poetry entrants wrote essays about local history.
questions.explanation: The finalists are seniors in the contest, so all five wrote about local history, and two of them entered the poetry contest. Nothing limits who else entered the poetry contest.

questions.passage: Students who eat breakfast every day earn higher grades, on average, than students who skip it. So if the school served a free breakfast to every student, grades at the school would rise.
questions.stem: The argument's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument:
options: fails to say how much a free breakfast program would cost the school
relies on an average that may hide wide differences among students
ignores that what leads students to eat breakfast may also raise grades
takes for granted that grades are the best measure of what students learn
assumes that every student would like the breakfast the school serves
questions.explanation: Families who make sure children eat breakfast may also help with study and sleep, which could explain the grades; a free meal would not supply those. The cost of the program does not bear on whether grades would rise.

questions.passage: Some economists claim that raising the minimum wage always reduces employment. But when Westland raised its minimum wage last year, employment in its restaurants, which pay many minimum-wage workers, grew faster than in neighboring states. This does not show that raising the minimum wage never costs jobs. It does show, however, that such raises do not always reduce employment.
questions.stem: The claim that Westland's experience does not show that raising the minimum wage never costs jobs plays which one of the following roles in the argument?
options: It limits the conclusion the argument draws from its evidence.
It is a concession that undermines the argument's own conclusion.
It states the position that the argument sets out to refute.
It is evidence that the argument offers against the economists.
It is the main conclusion that the argument is meant to establish.
questions.explanation: The sentence says what the evidence does not prove, narrowing the conclusion to the claim that raises do not always cut jobs. It does not count against that conclusion; it sets its limits.

questions.passage: Jamal has served as treasurer of the Oakmont Garden Club, and anyone who has served as the club's treasurer understands the club's finances. So Jamal is qualified to review the club's annual budget.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
options: Anyone qualified to review the club's budget understands the club's finances.
Most former treasurers of the club have reviewed its budget at some point.
Jamal understands the club's finances better than any other club member.
Anyone who understands the club's finances is qualified to review its budget.
Only those who have served as the club's treasurer may review its budget.
questions.explanation: Jamal understands the finances, and if everyone who does is qualified, he is qualified. The reversed claim, that qualified reviewers understand the finances, does not let the conclusion follow.

questions.passage: A national survey found that people who live in cities walk more each day, on average, than people who live in rural areas. Yet rural residents, on average, have better cardiovascular fitness than city residents.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
options: Cardiovascular fitness declines with age among both city and rural residents.
Rural residents are far more likely than city dwellers to do physically demanding work.
More city residents than rural residents took part in the national survey.
City residents are more likely than rural residents to own a car of their own.
Rural residents often say in surveys that they would like to walk more than they now do.
questions.explanation: Demanding physical work can build fitness that walking does not, so rural residents could walk less yet be fitter. Car ownership would, if anything, make the city walking figure harder to explain.

questions.passage: Principle: A teacher should give a student extra time on an assignment only if the student asks for it before the due date and the delay results from circumstances beyond the student's control.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
options: Mr. Dunn should give Ana extra time, since her illness was beyond her control, though she asked late.
Mr. Cole should give Jo extra time, since she asked on time, even though she forgot the deadline.
Ms. Lee should give Raj extra time, since he asked before the due date and his laptop was stolen.
Ms. Park should not give Tim extra time, though he asked early because his flight was canceled.
Mr. Ortiz should not give Kim extra time, since she asked after the due date, though she was ill.
questions.explanation: The principle states conditions that must be met, so it supports refusing Kim, who asked late. It never says a teacher must grant time when both conditions are met, so it does not support the judgment about Raj.

questions.passage: The Westbrook Gazette is the most reliable newspaper in the region. We know this because the Gazette's own annual report states that its reporting is more accurate than that of any of its competitors.
questions.stem: The argument's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument:
options: assumes that a paper's past accuracy guarantees its future accuracy
treats the size of a paper's readership as a sign of accuracy
relies on a source with an obvious interest in its conclusion
attacks the paper's competitors instead of giving evidence
draws a conclusion about every paper from a single example
questions.explanation: The only evidence is the Gazette's praise of itself, and the Gazette gains from that claim. The argument never mentions readership or rival papers' faults.

questions.passage: The proposal to ban gas leaf blowers in residential areas deserves support, though not for the reason usually given. Opponents are right that leaf blowers are no louder than many lawn mowers. But gas leaf blowers give off far more pollution per hour of use than gas mowers do, and that fact alone justifies the ban.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?
options: The ban on gas leaf blowers in residential areas should be supported.
Gas lawn mowers should also be banned in the town's residential areas.
Noise is the reason usually given for banning gas leaf blowers in towns.
Gas leaf blowers are no louder than many of the lawn mowers people use.
Gas leaf blowers pollute far more per hour of use than gas lawn mowers do.
questions.explanation: The pollution comparison is the reason given for the first sentence's claim that the ban deserves support. The argument does not propose banning mowers.

questions.passage: In a taste study, volunteers who were told that a wine was expensive rated it as tasting better than volunteers who were told that the same wine was cheap. Brain scans showed more activity in regions linked to pleasure among the volunteers told the higher price.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
options: Expensive wines taste better than inexpensive wines to most people.
Brain scans are the most reliable means of measuring how food tastes.
No one can tell an expensive wine from a cheap one by taste alone.
Beliefs about price can affect the pleasure people take in a product.
Volunteers told the low price disliked the wine they were given.
questions.explanation: The wine was the same, so only the stated price differed, and both ratings and pleasure activity rose with it. The study used one wine, so it cannot show that expensive wines taste better or that no one can tell wines apart.

questions.passage: Archaeologist: The stone tools found at the Kel site were made by people who traveled there from the coast. The tools are made of a kind of flint that is found nowhere within 200 kilometers of Kel except along the coast.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the archaeologist's argument?
options: Some of the tools found at the Kel site are made of local kinds of stone.
No evidence has been found that coastal flint was traded inland then.
Flint tools wear down faster than tools made of other kinds of stone.
The coastal flint is harder than any other flint found in the region.
The Kel site was occupied by people for several hundred years.
questions.explanation: The main alternative is that the flint reached Kel by trade while the toolmakers stayed put; evidence against such trade strengthens the claim. Local stone tools say nothing about who made the flint ones.

questions.passage: Public health official: Requiring restaurants to list calorie counts on their menus will lead diners to choose lower-calorie meals, since diners now underestimate how many calories restaurant meals contain.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the official's argument depends?
options: Most restaurants serve meals with more calories than a typical diner needs.
Restaurants will reduce the calories in their meals once counts are listed.
The diners who underestimate calories the most are mostly those who often eat out.
Calorie counts are the only information diners use when choosing a meal.
Some diners who learn a meal has more calories than they thought would skip it.
questions.explanation: If diners who learn the true count would order just the same, listing counts would not change their choices. Restaurants cutting calories is a different route that the argument does not rely on.

questions.passage: Some of the best-paid workers in Harlow are software engineers, and some software engineers in Harlow work from home. So some of the best-paid workers in Harlow work from home.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the argument?
options: It assumes that working from home tends to lower a worker's pay.
It treats being well paid as though it were the same as being skilled.
The engineers who are best paid may not be the ones who work from home.
It relies on information about the workers of only a single city.
It concludes that all workers share a trait that only some workers have.
questions.explanation: Two overlapping "some" groups need not share any members: the well-paid engineers could all work in offices. The conclusion is itself a "some" claim, so the argument does not generalize to all workers.

questions.passage: Every apartment in the Linden Building has a balcony, and no apartment with a balcony is allowed a grill. So none of the apartments in the Linden Building is allowed a grill.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
options: Every car on the lot has winter tires, and no car with winter tires may be sold before March. So no car on the lot may be sold before March.
Most cars on the lot have winter tires, and no car with winter tires may be sold before March. So no car on the lot may be sold before March.
Every car on the lot has winter tires, and some cars with winter tires may not be sold before March. So some cars on the lot may not be.
No car on the lot has winter tires, and no car with winter tires may be sold before March. So every car on the lot may be sold before March.
Every car with winter tires is on the lot, and no car on the lot may be sold before March. So no car without them may be sold before March.
questions.explanation: The building argument runs: all A are B, no B is C, so no A is C, which is valid; the first car argument has exactly that form. The others change a quantifier or reverse a term and do not follow.

questions.passage: Philosopher: Some say that because we cannot foresee the long-term consequences of our actions, we cannot be blamed for them. But if that were so, no one could be blamed for anything, since every action has long-term consequences that no one can foresee. Yet we rightly blame people for many of their actions.
questions.stem: The philosopher's argument proceeds by:
options: arguing that the long-term consequences of actions can in fact usually be foreseen
offering a case in which consequences were foreseen in order to refute a generalization
distinguishing two senses of the word blame that the opposing view runs together
showing that a view, if accepted, leads to a conclusion that is clearly unacceptable
questioning the motives of the people who hold the view that the philosopher opposes
questions.explanation: The philosopher grants the view for argument's sake, shows it would excuse everyone, and rejects it because we rightly blame people. No particular case is offered, and foreseeability is not disputed.

questions.passage: Reading scores at Fairview Elementary rose sharply in the two years after the school replaced its printed textbooks with tablets. The district concludes that switching to tablets improved students' reading.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
options: Teachers at Fairview needed several weeks of training to use the tablets well.
Two years ago the state adopted an easier test, and scores rose at nearly every school.
Some students at Fairview read far more on their tablets than they ever did in printed books.
Fairview's math scores rose by less over those two years than its reading scores.
The tablets cost the district more than the printed textbooks they replaced.
questions.explanation: If an easier test raised scores almost everywhere, Fairview's rise is no sign that tablets helped. More reading on tablets would, if anything, support the district.

questions.passage: Moths of a certain species are either pale or dark. Relative to their numbers, birds catch far more dark moths than pale ones in woodland where the tree bark is pale. In woodland where the bark is darkened with soot, birds catch far more pale moths than dark ones, again relative to their numbers.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
options: Dark moths now outnumber pale moths in woodland darkened by soot.
Birds prefer the taste of dark moths to the taste of pale moths.
Moths choose to rest on tree bark that matches their own color.
Soot in the air harms the health of pale moths more than dark moths.
Birds find it harder to spot moths that match the bark they rest on.
questions.explanation: In each woodland the moths that contrast with the bark are caught more often, which fits the idea that matching moths are harder to see. The statements are about catch rates, not about which moths are more numerous.

questions.passage: Historian: The letters said to have been written by the merchant Corvin could not have been written by him. The letters mention the harbor fire of 1612, and records show that Corvin died in 1609.
questions.stem: The historian's argument requires assuming which one of the following?
options: Corvin was not known to write letters to anyone outside his own family.
The harbor fire of 1612 destroyed most of the town's written records.
The letters do not refer to the fire as an event that had not yet happened.
Whoever wrote the letters lived in the harbor town at the time of the fire.
The records of Corvin's death are the only ones surviving from that period.
questions.explanation: If the letters described the fire as a danger still to come, a writer who died in 1609 could have mentioned it, and the argument would fail. Where the writer lived is not needed.

questions.passage: Toxicologist: Twelve studies have examined the effect of the new pesticide on honeybees, and none found that it shortens the bees' lives. So the pesticide is harmless to honeybees.
questions.stem: The toxicologist's reasoning is flawed because it:
options: overlooks harm the pesticide could do without shortening bees' lives
relies on too few studies to support any conclusion about honeybees
fails to say which organizations paid for the twelve studies
assumes that pesticides harmless to honeybees are harmless to people
takes for granted that all twelve studies measured lifespan the same way
questions.explanation: The studies looked only at lifespan, while a pesticide could still impair foraging, navigation or reproduction. Twelve studies is not too few for a claim about lifespan; the gap is between lifespan and harm in general.

questions.passage: If the new exhibit is reviewed favorably, it will draw large crowds. The exhibit drew large crowds, so it must have been reviewed favorably.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in the argument above is most similar to that in which one of the following?
options: If the orchard gets enough rain, it will give a large harvest. It did not give a large harvest, so it did not get enough rain.
If the orchard gets enough rain, it gives a large harvest, and it always gets enough rain, so it always gives a large harvest.
The orchard will give a large harvest only if it gets enough rain. It gave a large harvest, so it must have had enough rain.
If the orchard gets enough rain, it will give a large harvest. It gave a large harvest, so it must have had enough rain.
If the orchard gets enough rain, it will give a large harvest. It did not get enough rain, so it will not give a large one.
questions.explanation: The exhibit argument infers the condition from the result it guarantees, and so does the large-harvest argument with the if-clause. Reasoning from no rain is a different flaw, and the only-if and no-large-harvest versions are valid.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
options: Performers lost the ability to improvise once composers wrote out their own cadenzas.
The rise of written cadenzas traded performers' freedom for a coherence listeners gained.
Soloists today should return to improvising their cadenzas instead of playing written ones.
Written cadenzas are artistically superior to the improvised cadenzas of the past.
Music historians have exaggerated how often eighteenth-century soloists improvised.
questions.explanation: The author grants the historians' loss but adds a gain, concluding that the history is "better told as an exchange than as a loss." The final paragraph rejects both a return to improvising and the view that one practice is simply better.

questions.stem: According to the passage, eighteenth-century composers usually:
options: objected when soloists improvised on themes from the movement
chose famous performers to write the cadenzas for their works
wrote out a complete cadenza for each movement of their concertos
required soloists to prepare their cadenzas well in advance of a concert
marked where a cadenza began and left its content to the performer
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says composers "usually marked only where the cadenza should begin" and left what was played to the performer. Writing out cadenzas came later.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the music historians' view described in the second paragraph is best described as:
options: indifference to whether its account of the change is correct
suspicion that its supporters favor written music for personal reasons
agreement that it is accurate as far as it goes, but not complete
complete rejection of its claim that anything at all was lost in the change
uncritical acceptance of its account of how the cadenza changed
questions.explanation: The third paragraph opens: "That account is not wrong, but it is incomplete." The author keeps the loss and adds what was gained, so the view is neither rejected nor simply accepted.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that an improvised cadenza in the eighteenth century was most likely to differ from a carefully composed one in that the improvised cadenza:
options: relied more on familiar figures than on developing the themes
was more difficult for the soloist to play than a written one
was less admired by eighteenth-century audiences than a written one
lasted longer than a written cadenza for the same movement would
drew on themes from movements other than the one being played
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says improvisers under pressure "tended to rely on familiar figures," while a composer at a desk could develop the movement's own material. Nothing is said about length or difficulty.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
options: A historical claim is stated, evidence against it is presented, and the claim is withdrawn by its author.
A problem in performance is identified, several solutions are evaluated, and one solution is recommended.
A practice is described, two opposing accounts of it are compared, and the older account is shown to be false.
A practice is described, a common account of its change is qualified, and a reframing is offered.
A change is described, its causes are listed in order of importance, and its effects are left for later study.
questions.explanation: The passage describes the eighteenth-century cadenza, gives the historians' account of loss, adds what that account omits, and ends by recasting the history as an exchange. No account is shown false or withdrawn.

questions.stem: As it is used in the third paragraph, the word "culmination" most nearly means:
options: a summary written after the music is done
a high point that completes what came before
a passage that repeats the opening exactly
a test of the soloist's technical skill
a sudden break from the rest of the movement
questions.explanation: The admired cadenzas "read less as interruptions than as a culmination," developing material the movement had only suggested, so they complete it. A break is what "interruptions" describes.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the change in the cadenza as the author describes it?
options: A city replaces its old library with a new one that holds more books and keeps every service the old one offered.
Architects abandon hand drawing for computer design, which produces exactly the same buildings at a lower cost.
A sport changes its rules to forbid a tactic, and the change is reversed after players and fans complain.
A cook gives up written recipes and improvises every dish, so that meals become both more varied and more consistent.
Troupes that once improvised scenes adopt written scripts, losing spontaneity but gaining tightly built plots.
questions.explanation: The author's point is an exchange: performers lost a freedom while listeners gained coherence. The troupe gives up spontaneity for well-built plots, a trade of the same kind; the library and design cases involve no loss at all.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
options: Judges should explain the law to jurors in their own words instead of reading written instructions.
Model jury instructions are precise enough that most jurors understand the law they are asked to apply.
Jury instructions should be carefully rewritten in plain language so that jurors apply the law intended.
Appeals based on new wording make it impractical for courts to adopt plain-language jury instructions.
Technical legal terms carry connotations that everyday words were chosen by drafters to avoid.
questions.explanation: The passage presents the research on misunderstanding, answers both objections and ends by saying careful rewriting is the only way to ensure jurors apply the law intended. It treats the appeal problem as temporary, not decisive.

questions.stem: According to the passage, studies using mock jurors found that rewritten instructions:
options: improved comprehension without changing the legal rule explained
led jurors to reach different verdicts than the original ones did
were understood better by lawyers than the original instructions
were preferred by jurors although they understood them no better
reduced the time jurors needed to reach a unanimous verdict
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says rewritten instructions "produced markedly better comprehension without changing the legal rule being explained." Nothing is said about verdicts or deliberation time.

questions.stem: The author's response to the first objection relies on which one of the following?
options: Everyday words carry no connotations that could mislead the jurors who hear them.
Jurors understand everyday words exactly as the drafters of instructions intend.
Plain-language instructions have never been challenged in an appeal of a verdict.
The research doubts that technical terms convey their meaning to jurors.
Technical legal terms were originally chosen without any concern for their accuracy.
questions.explanation: The author answers that the objection "assumes that technical terms convey their intended meaning to jurors, which is exactly what the research calls into question." The author does not claim everyday words are free of connotations.

questions.stem: The author regards the second objection to rewriting instructions as:
options: decisive enough that courts should delay rewriting until it has been answered
stronger than the first but naming a temporary cost, not a lasting flaw
weaker than the first because it rests on a misreading of the research
irrelevant, since appeals have no bearing on how jury instructions are worded
convincing to judges but of little interest to people who study comprehension
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says the second objection "has more force" but "describes a cost of transition rather than a permanent defect," citing jurisdictions where such appeals became uncommon.

questions.stem: The author uses the phrase "the precision of legal drafting" in the first paragraph primarily to suggest that the model instructions are:
options: written to be read silently rather than aloud
precise only when a judge explains them to the jury
carefully drafted but legally out of date in many courts
less exact than the plain-language rewrites have proved
exact in a way that suits lawyers better than jurors
questions.explanation: The phrase is followed by long sentences, technical terms and double negatives "that a lawyer parses easily and a juror may not parse at all," so the precision is of a kind that serves lawyers.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most support the author's response to the second objection?
options: Most judges say that they prefer the model instructions because they are familiar with their wording.
Drafting committees for model instructions have rarely included people trained in testing comprehension.
In a state that adopted plain-language instructions, appeals over the wording fell within a few years.
Mock jurors who heard plain-language instructions reached verdicts more quickly than other mock jurors did.
Some appeals courts have overturned verdicts because a judge departed from the model instructions.
questions.explanation: The author answers the practical objection by saying appeals on new wording become uncommon after a transition; evidence that appeals fell quickly in a state that switched supports that answer. Overturned verdicts would support the objection instead.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the final paragraph is to:
options: draw from the objections a lesson about how to carry out rewriting
introduce a new objection to plain-language instructions and answer it
concede that the objections show plain language is a concession to jurors
summarize the research that the second paragraph described in detail
argue that model instructions should be kept until new research is done
questions.explanation: The paragraph begins "What the objections do show is that rewriting should be done with care" and then describes how. It explicitly denies that plain language is a concession to jurors' limitations.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?
options: Large trees should be left standing during logging because they feed seedlings through fungal networks.
Popular accounts of forests as cooperative communities have been proved false by recent experiments.
Mycorrhizal fungi do not connect the roots of different trees in mature forests as many have believed.
Claims that trees share resources through fungal networks outrun the evidence and need field tests.
Fungi rather than trees decide where carbon goes in a forest's underground networks.
questions.explanation: The passage reports critics who accept that networks exist but say the evidence does not show transfers large or directed enough to matter, and it ends by calling for tests in mature forests. It does not deny the networks or claim the popular accounts have been disproved.

questions.stem: According to the passage, mycorrhizal fungi provide trees with:
options: protection from shade cast by larger nearby trees
water and mineral nutrients gathered from the soil
seeds carried from one part of the forest to another
sugars that the fungi make from the soil's minerals
carbon taken from the roots of neighboring seedlings
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the fungi "draw sugars from the trees and in return deliver water and mineral nutrients." The sugars go from the trees to the fungi, not the other way.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is mentioned in the passage as a reason the critics give for doubting the evidence?
options: The seedlings in most experiments were of a different species from the trees.
The fungi involved in the experiments were of a species rare in forests.
The researchers who did the experiments disagreed about their results.
The experiments measured water transfer but never carbon transfer.
Carbon detected in a second tree might have moved there through the soil.
