questions.passage: Anthropologist: The pottery found at the coastal site was made in the inland valley, since its clay contains a mineral that occurs naturally only in the valley's riverbeds.
questions.stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?
options: Pottery from the valley was finer than any pottery made on the coast.
Potters in the valley traded regularly with people living on the coast.
No pottery of this kind has been found anywhere else along the coast.
Coastal potters did not bring valley clay home and shape it there.
The coastal site was occupied by people for many centuries in a row.
questions.explanation: If coastal potters had brought valley clay home and shaped it there, the mineral would be in pots made on the coast, and the argument would fail. Regular trade is not required: the claim is only about where the pots were made.

questions.passage: Policy analyst: Requiring every new downtown building to have a green roof will lower summer temperatures downtown, because green roofs stay much cooler in summer than conventional roofs do.
questions.stem: The analyst's argument requires assuming which one of the following?
options: Summer temperatures downtown are higher than those in the nearby suburbs.
Enough new buildings will go up downtown for their roofs to matter.
Most downtown buildings will be torn down and replaced within ten years.
Green roofs cost more to build than conventional roofs of the same size do.
Green roofs also reduce the amount of runoff from heavy summer rainstorms.
questions.explanation: If only a handful of new buildings were ever built, their roofs could not change downtown temperatures. Replacing most buildings within ten years is far more than the argument needs.

questions.passage: Anyone who has completed the food safety course may sort donations at the Riverside Food Bank. Leon volunteers at the food bank. So Leon may sort donations there.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
options: The food safety course takes only a single afternoon to complete.
Everyone who may sort donations has completed the food safety course.
Some volunteers at the food bank have completed the food safety course.
Leon has volunteered at the Riverside Food Bank for more than a year.
Every volunteer at the food bank has completed the food safety course.
questions.explanation: If every volunteer has completed the course, Leon has, and the first premise then lets him sort donations. That some volunteers have done so leaves Leon open.

questions.passage: Any runner who wins a regional final qualifies for this year's national championship. Priya has won every race she has entered this season. So Priya qualifies for this year's national championship.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
options: Priya trains with a former national champion.
Every national runner won a regional final.
Priya entered a regional final this season.
Most regional finalists have won earlier races.
Priya has entered more races than any rival.
questions.explanation: If Priya entered a regional final this season, she won it, since she won every race she entered, and winning one qualifies her. The claim about every national runner states a requirement, not a guarantee.

questions.passage: Every bird species on Corran Island that eats seeds is protected by law. The island's ground finch is not protected by law. Therefore, the ground finch does not nest in the island's coastal forest.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
options: Every bird species on the island that nests in the coastal forest eats seeds.
No seed-eating bird species on the island nests outside the coastal forest.
Every bird species protected by law on the island nests in the coastal forest.
The ground finch eats insects and other small animals rather than seeds.
Some bird species that nest in the island's coastal forest eat insects.
questions.explanation: The finch is unprotected, so it does not eat seeds; if every coastal forest nester eats seeds, the finch cannot nest there. Knowing it eats insects still says nothing about where it nests.

questions.passage: The town of Ferris credits its new countdown crosswalk signals, which show pedestrians the seconds left to cross, with a drop in pedestrian injuries at its downtown intersections.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the town's claim?
options: Many pedestrians said in a survey that they liked the new signals.
Some intersections downtown have no crossing signals of any kind.
Countdown signals have been common in large cities for years.
Injuries did not fall at intersections that kept the old signals.
The new signals were paid for by a state traffic safety grant.
questions.explanation: If intersections without the new signals saw no drop, something other than a general trend explains the fall where the signals went in. How the signals were paid for bears on nothing.

questions.passage: Studies have found that students who take music lessons score higher on math tests than students who do not. A school board concludes that requiring music lessons for all students would raise math scores.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
options: Music lessons teach students to count beats and to read musical patterns.
Families who pay for music lessons tend to pay for math tutoring too.
Some of the students who take music lessons do not enjoy them.
Many students who do well in math also play sports after school.
Math tests at the board's schools were revised two years ago.
questions.explanation: If music students also get math tutoring, the tutoring may explain their scores, and required music lessons would not supply it. Counting beats offers a way lessons might help, which supports the board.

questions.passage: Although the Wescott Library stopped charging fines for overdue books last year, the share of books returned late fell.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
options: Many other libraries that ended fines saw more books returned late than before.
The patrons who returned books late were most often students at the college.
The library's fines for overdue books had been small even before they ended.
The library bought more new books last year than in any year before that.
When it ended fines, the library began texting reminders before each due date.
questions.explanation: Reminders before the due date could cut late returns even without fines, so both facts fit. Other libraries seeing more late returns makes Wescott's result more puzzling, not less.

questions.passage: Company spokesperson: Our delivery drones will cut delivery times in the city, since drones fly straight to their destinations instead of following the streets.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would it be most useful to determine in order to evaluate the spokesperson's argument?
options: How the price of a drone compares with the price of a delivery van
How many customers would rather pick up their packages in person
Whether city rules let drones fly the direct routes they would need
Whether the drones make less noise than the company's delivery vans
Whether the drones were designed by the company's own engineers
questions.explanation: The argument relies on direct flight; if rules force drones around restricted areas, the advantage may vanish. Noise and price do not bear on delivery time.

questions.passage: Paleontologist: The giant flightless birds of Tarran Island died out because the first human settlers hunted them. Their bones disappear from the island's fossil record within a century of the settlers' arrival.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the paleontologist's argument?
options: Bird bones in the settlers' oldest refuse heaps bear butchery marks.
The settlers on the island grew crops as well as hunting for food.
Tarran Island lies far from the nearest mainland and other islands.
The birds' bones are well preserved in several of the island's caves.
The birds were among the largest ever to have lived on any island.
questions.explanation: Butchered bones show the settlers killed and ate the birds, which ties the extinction to hunting rather than mere timing. The birds' size and the island's remoteness do not bear on why they vanished.

questions.passage: Economist: The cities that raised their hotel taxes last year had fewer tourists last year than the year before. So raising hotel taxes drives tourists away.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
options: Some of those cities used the new tax revenue to pay for museums and parks.
Tourists who visited those cities spent more each day than tourists had before.
The cities that raised their taxes had more hotels than most other cities do.
Those cities raised hotel taxes because tourist numbers were already falling.
Most tourists who visited those cities stayed for two or more nights in a row.
questions.explanation: If falling numbers led the cities to raise taxes, the decline came first and the taxes cannot explain it. How the revenue was spent says nothing about why tourists stayed away.

questions.passage: I asked three of my neighbors whether they would pay more for faster internet service, and all three said no. So hardly anyone in the city would pay more for faster internet service.
questions.stem: The argument's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument:
options: fails to say how much faster the service would become
draws a broad conclusion from far too small a sample
assumes the neighbors know what faster service means
treats a preference as though it were a requirement
assumes internet prices in the city will stay the same
questions.explanation: Three neighbors cannot stand for a whole city's residents. How much faster the service would be does not affect that gap in the reasoning.

questions.passage: The Brightwater Orchestra is one of the finest orchestras in the world. So each of its musicians must be among the finest players of their instruments in the world.
questions.stem: The argument's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument:
options: assumes the orchestra will remain among the finest in the future
confuses the fame of an orchestra with the quality of its playing
fails to name any of the musicians who play in the orchestra
relies on a ranking of orchestras without saying who made it
assumes each part of a whole has a quality that the whole has
questions.explanation: A fine orchestra can owe its quality to how its players work together, so its excellence does not pass to every member. The argument says nothing about fame.

questions.passage: Most voters in the district say that they want lower taxes. So most voters in the district will support Senator Lowe's plan to cut the sales tax.
questions.stem: The argument's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument:
options: confuses a cut in the sales tax with a cut in government spending
treats the district's voters as typical of voters in the whole state
overlooks that voters may want lower taxes but not this particular cut
takes for granted that the senator is popular among the district's voters
assumes that the senator's plan will pass in the state legislature
questions.explanation: Voters who want lower taxes might prefer cutting a different tax or object to what this cut would cost them, so a general wish does not show support for this plan. The argument says nothing about the rest of the state.

questions.passage: Either the city builds a new stadium or the team will leave town. The team leaving would be a disaster for the city, so the city must build the stadium.
questions.stem: The argument's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument:
options: assumes without support that these are the only two outcomes
relies on the claims of the team's owners about the old stadium
concludes that the stadium will be built because the city wants it
fails to say how much the new stadium would cost the city to build
assumes that the team is popular with most of the city's residents
questions.explanation: The city might renovate the old stadium or reach another deal, so the stark choice is not established. The stadium's cost would matter to a fuller debate but not to this gap.

questions.passage: Millions of people take vitamin C to ward off colds. A remedy used by so many people must work.
questions.stem: The argument's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument:
options: relies on people who profit from the sale of vitamin C
fails to say which brands of vitamin C people tend to take
assumes that vitamin C has no side effects for most people
treats how widely a remedy is used as proof that it works
draws a conclusion about all vitamins from a single vitamin
questions.explanation: Many people can use a remedy that does nothing, so popularity is not evidence of effect. The conclusion concerns vitamin C only, not all vitamins.

questions.passage: The new parking rules have sent many small shops' customers to the mall on the edge of town. Since the mall's owners gave money to the council members who passed the rules, the rules were clearly meant to help the mall.
questions.stem: The argument's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument:
options: assumes that the mall's prices are lower than those of the shops
takes an effect and a donation as proof of the rules' purpose
relies on the shop owners' own account of their lost customers
treats every council member as having voted the same way
fails to say how many small shops have lost customers to the mall
questions.explanation: That the rules help the mall, and that its owners gave money, are consistent with the rules having been passed for other reasons. The number of shops affected does not touch the inference about purpose.

questions.passage: Every train that stops at Elm Street also stops at Grand Central. No express train stops at Grand Central. The 7:15 train stops at Elm Street.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
options: The 7:15 train stops only at those two stations.
Some express trains stop at Elm Street.
No train that stops at Grand Central is late.
Every Grand Central train stops at Elm Street.
The 7:15 train is not an express train.
questions.explanation: The 7:15 stops at Elm Street, so it stops at Grand Central, and no express stops there. The statements do not say it stops nowhere else.

questions.passage: In the Harlan region, wells near large farms have higher nitrate levels than wells far from any farm. Wells near farms that switched to slow-release fertilizer ten years ago now have nitrate levels close to those of wells far from any farm.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
options: Most farms in the Harlan region now use slow-release fertilizer.
Slow-release fertilizer gives farms larger harvests than others do.
The fertilizer farms use can affect nitrate levels in nearby wells.
All of the nitrates in the region's wells come from farm fertilizer.
Wells far from farms are unaffected by the amount of rain that falls.
questions.explanation: Wells near farms that changed fertilizer now resemble wells far from farms, which supports a link between fertilizer type and nitrates. Nothing is said about harvests or how many farms switched.

questions.passage: Every senior at Ridgeline High who is on the honor roll has taken calculus. No senior who has taken calculus is in the beginning statistics class. Some seniors in the beginning statistics class are on the debate team.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true?
options: A senior on the honor roll is in the beginning statistics class.
Every senior who has taken calculus is on the honor roll.
Some seniors in beginning statistics are not on the debate team.
Some seniors on the debate team have already taken calculus.
No senior on the debate team is also on the honor roll.
questions.explanation: An honor roll senior has taken calculus, and no one who has taken calculus is in beginning statistics. The debate team can include calculus students who are not in that class, so some debate team members may well have taken calculus.

questions.passage: The Kestrel Award is given to one author each year. Every previous winner has been a novelist. This year's winner is a poet who has never written a novel.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
options: Next year's winner of the award will be a novelist once again.
No poet had ever been nominated for the award before this year.
Some earlier winners of the award also wrote poetry.
This year's winner did not win the award in any earlier year.
Every novelist who has won the award wrote only novels.
questions.explanation: Every earlier winner was a novelist, and this year's winner has never written a novel, so she cannot have been an earlier winner. Nothing is said about nominations, so poets may have been nominated before.

questions.passage: After the town of Bly installed speed cameras on Ash Road, average speeds there fell sharply. On nearby Birch Road, which has no cameras, average speeds rose slightly over the same period, and the amount of traffic increased.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
options: Traffic on Ash Road fell by exactly the amount that Birch Road's rose.
Some drivers may have moved from Ash Road to Birch Road after the change.
The cameras went on Ash Road because it had the most crashes in town.
Speed cameras lead drivers to slow down on every road in a town.
Drivers on Birch Road are less careful than the drivers who use Ash Road.
questions.explanation: More traffic on the nearby road without cameras fits drivers moving to avoid them, though the statements do not prove it, which is why the key is hedged. Speeds on Birch Road rose, so cameras did not slow every road.

questions.passage: A survey of hospital nurses found that those working twelve-hour shifts reported more medication errors than those working eight-hour shifts. Among nurses on twelve-hour shifts, most reported errors occurred in the last four hours of a shift.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
options: Hospitals should not let any nurse work a twelve-hour shift.
Nurses on eight-hour shifts make no errors in their last hours.
Less experienced nurses tend to choose the twelve-hour shifts.
Medication errors are the most common errors made in hospitals.
Fatigue late in long shifts may contribute to medication errors.
questions.explanation: Errors clustered in the final hours of long shifts suggest that something about those hours, such as tiredness, plays a part. A policy against long shifts goes beyond what the survey shows.

questions.passage: Any student who misses the deadline loses points. Ana missed the deadline. So Ana loses points.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
options: Any car parked here after six is towed. Ben's car is not towed. So no car is parked here.
Any car parked here after six is towed. Ben's car was not parked here then. So it is not towed.
Any car parked here after six is towed. Ben's car was parked here after six. So it is towed.
Most cars parked here after six are towed. Ben's car was parked here then. So it is towed.
Any car parked here after six is towed. Ben's car was towed. So it was parked here after six.
questions.explanation: Both arguments apply a rule to a case that meets its condition. Reasoning from the towing back to the parking, or from not parking to not towing, reverses the rule.

questions.passage: Some economists are optimists, and some optimists are poor investors. So some economists are poor investors.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in the argument above is most similar to that in which one of the following?
options: Some painters are teachers, and some teachers are poets. So some painters are poets.
All painters are teachers, and all teachers are poets. So all painters are poets.
No painters are teachers, and some teachers are poets. So no painters are poets.
Some painters are teachers, and all teachers are poets. So some painters are poets.
All painters are teachers, and some teachers are poets. So all painters are poets.
questions.explanation: Two "some" claims that share a middle group cannot link the outer groups, since the overlaps may differ, and the painter argument makes the same mistake. The versions with "all" in the right place are valid.

questions.passage: Principle: A company should tell its customers about a defect in a product as soon as it learns that the defect could cause injury.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
options: Dalt Motors acted rightly in delaying notice of a brake fault it knew could cause a crash.
Corin Foods acted wrongly in announcing a defect before confirming it could cause any injury.
Belmore Tools acted rightly in delaying notice of a scratch in the paint until it had a fix ready.
Arlo Toys acted wrongly in waiting a month to report a loose part it knew a child could choke on.
Easton Phones acted wrongly in disclosing a battery flaw that posed no risk to anyone at all.
questions.explanation: Arlo knew the part could injure a child and still waited, which the principle forbids. The principle is silent on defects that cannot cause injury, so it supports no verdict on the scratch or the battery.

questions.passage: Librarian: We should keep the reading room open on holidays. Many patrons who rely on the library's computers have no other place to use one, and opening the room costs little.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the librarian's argument?
options: A public service should be offered only if most of the residents in the area actually use it.
A service should stay open when closing it denies people a needed resource and opening costs little.
Public buildings should close on holidays so that the city can save money on its energy bills.
A library should spend most of its budget on computers rather than on new books and magazines.
A public library should be open on every day that its staff members are willing to come in and work.
questions.explanation: The librarian gives two reasons, patrons' need and the low cost, and the principle ties those two conditions to staying open. Staff willingness plays no part in the librarian's reasoning.

questions.passage: If the bakery wins the contract, it will hire more staff. If it hires more staff, it will need a bigger kitchen. The bakery will not need a bigger kitchen, so it did not win the contract.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
options: If Nadia gets the grant, she will go to Peru or Chile. She will not go to Chile, so she will be going to Peru after all.
If Nadia gets the grant, she will go to Peru. If she goes, she will need a passport. She needs one, so she must have got the grant.
If Nadia goes to Peru, she will need a passport. She will need a passport, so she will be going to Peru after all.
If Nadia gets the grant, she will go to Peru. If she goes, she will need a passport. She did not get it, so she will not need one.
If Nadia gets the grant, she will go to Peru. If she goes, she will need a passport. She will not need one, so she did not get the grant.
questions.explanation: Both arguments chain two conditionals and then deny the final result to deny the first condition. Reasoning from needing a passport or from not getting the grant reverses a conditional.

questions.passage: Principle: When two people both have a claim to a scarce resource, it should go to the one who would be harmed more by not getting it, unless the other has a prior agreement entitling them to it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
options: Pia and Raj both want the last seat on the bus, so they should take turns sitting in it.
Sam would enjoy the last concert ticket more than Tia would, so the ticket should go to Sam.
Kim's lease guarantees her the last parking space, so it should go to her, though Lou needs it more.
Mo asked for the study room first, so it should go to her, though Ned would be harmed more without it.
Lou needs the last parking space more than Kim does, so it should go to him despite Kim's lease.
questions.explanation: Kim's lease is a prior agreement, which is the principle's exception, so the space goes to her. Asking first is not an agreement, and enjoying something more is not being harmed more without it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
options: The cleaning dispute turns on evidence and judgment for both schools, and analysis now settles some cases.
Painters of earlier centuries finished most of their works with tinted glazes over the paint.
Complete cleaning is the scientific approach, and partial cleaning reflects the preferences of collectors.
Conservators should stop removing old varnish until better tests of glazes have been developed.
Old varnish should always be left in place because it protects paintings and deepens their colors.
questions.explanation: After setting out both schools, the passage denies that the dispute is science against taste, says both rely on evidence and judgment, and notes that new tests settle some cases. It calls the science-versus-taste description misleading.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the advocates of complete cleaning object that partly cleaned paintings often:
options: show colors harsher and more abrupt than the painter saw
turn darker within a few years than fully cleaned paintings
lose the thin glazes that soften the painter's transitions
take on a uniform golden tone that reflects later preferences
need to be varnished again more often than other paintings
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says partly cleaned pictures "often end up with a uniform golden tone" tied to later collectors' preferences. Lost glazes and harsh colors are the second school's worries about complete cleaning.

questions.stem: It can be inferred that members of the second school regard cleaning by stages as safe chiefly because it:
options: removes all of the old varnish more slowly than other methods do
lets the conservator stop before a glaze goes with the varnish
avoids the need for any chemical testing of the painting's layers
makes it possible to apply fresh varnish between each of the stages
allows a painting to keep the golden tone that collectors prefer
questions.explanation: The second school fears that glazes look like varnish and may be removed with it; pausing to judge the effect lets a conservator stop in time. The golden tone is what the first school complains of.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the final paragraph is to:
options: introduce a third school of conservators that rejects both other views
show that complete cleaning has been proved right by recent chemical tests
explain why traditional varnishes yellow and darken as they grow older
recommend that museums stop cleaning paintings until the dispute ends
correct a common account of the dispute and note how new tests bear on it
questions.explanation: The paragraph calls the science-versus-taste framing misleading and then says analysis has narrowed the disagreement where tests are clear. It does not side with either school.

questions.stem: In the final paragraph, the statement that "the choice largely makes itself" most nearly means that:
options: the choice of method no longer matters to the painting's look
conservators can choose whichever method they happen to prefer
the evidence leaves little room for a conservator's judgment
museum owners rather than conservators make the final choice
the painting will clean itself once the varnish is removed
questions.explanation: Where tests clearly show whether a layer is glaze or varnish, the right action follows from the evidence, so little is left to decide.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the two schools of conservators is best described as:
options: evenhanded, treating each as reasoning from evidence and judgment
dismissive of both as relying on taste rather than on evidence
favorable to partial cleaning as the safer way to treat paintings
favorable to complete cleaning as the more scientific of the two
impatient with both for failing to adopt chemical testing sooner
questions.explanation: The author says "both schools appeal to evidence" and both must make judgments the evidence does not settle, taking neither side.

questions.stem: Which one of the following cases best illustrates the situation described in the passage's last sentence?
options: A painting has no varnish at all, so the conservator applies a fresh coat of clear varnish.
A collector asks that a painting keep its golden tone, so the conservator leaves the varnish.
Tests show that a layer is plainly varnish, so the conservator removes it with confidence.
Tests on a layer are unclear, so the conservator must weigh the risk of stripping a glaze.
A painting's varnish has not yellowed, so the conservator decides not to clean it at all.
questions.explanation: The last sentence concerns cases where tests are unclear and the conservator must choose between leaving too much and taking too much. A clear test is the case in which the choice makes itself.

questions.stem: Which one of the following best describes the relationship between the two passages?
options: Passage A reports a survey's findings, and Passage B questions how the survey was conducted.
Passage A proposes a general policy, and Passage B reports one city's use of such a policy.
Passage A and Passage B offer two competing explanations of why drivers circle for parking.
Passage A describes a city's program, and Passage B argues that the program should be ended.
Passage A criticizes a policy that Passage B defends against the complaints of shop workers.
questions.explanation: Passage A argues that cities should price parking by demand; Passage B describes Delford doing that, with its results and complaints. Passage B neither argues for ending the program nor challenges A's explanation.

questions.stem: Which one of the following findings in Passage B most directly supports a claim made in Passage A?
options: Prices on many of the city's outlying blocks fell in the first year.
Business owners worried that higher prices would drive customers away.
Hourly workers said the prices took a large share of their wages.
The city offered discounted permits to low-wage downtown workers.
Time spent searching for parking downtown fell by about a third.
questions.explanation: Passage A says underpriced parking makes drivers circle; Delford's drop in search time after pricing by demand supports that claim. The permits and complaints are not claims Passage A makes.

questions.stem: Passage B mentions a concern that Passage A does not address. That concern is:
options: the fuel that drivers burn as they search for a place to park
the delays that full curbs can cause for buses on busy streets
the burden that higher prices place on workers paid by the hour
the traffic that drivers add while circling in search of a space
the empty spaces left on blocks where prices are kept too high
questions.explanation: Passage B reports hourly workers' complaints about the cost; Passage A discusses circling, fuel and bus delays but not who bears higher prices.

questions.stem: The author of Passage A would most likely regard Delford's change in its third year as:
options: compatible with the policy, since Passage A never requires one price
irrelevant, since Passage A is concerned only with outlying blocks
an admission that the policy increased traffic on the main streets
a betrayal of the policy, since every driver must pay the same price
proof that pricing by demand cannot work in a city the size of Delford
questions.explanation: Passage A asks only that block prices follow demand so spaces stay open; it never requires a single price for every driver, so a targeted discount funded from the revenue does not contradict it. The other options misstate Passage A or claim results neither passage reports.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine Passage B's report as support for Passage A's argument?
options: Some downtown shop workers in Delford began commuting to work by bus.
Delford set its prices to leave about one space in eight open on each block.
Prices on Delford's outlying blocks rose again in the program's third year.
Delford opened a large new garage downtown in the program's first year.
Delford's surveys of drivers were run by the city's own transport office.
questions.explanation: A new garage could explain the fall in searching on its own, so Delford's result would no longer show that demand pricing worked. Workers switching to the bus fits Passage A's point that drivers can travel another way.

questions.stem: The two passages most strongly suggest that their authors would agree with which one of the following?
options: Higher parking prices downtown will cause shops there to lose their customers.
Prices that follow demand can reduce the time drivers spend searching.
Discounted parking permits should be given to every worker in a downtown area.
Curb parking should be free on blocks where spaces sit empty most of the day.
Cities should set parking prices once and then leave them unchanged for years.
questions.explanation: Passage A predicts that demand pricing will end circling, and Passage B reports search time falling under it. Passage B notes that downtown sales did not fall, so neither author accepts that shops will lose customers.
